Empirical Research Plan: “Institutional Investors and Global Corporate Governance, 2000-2005”

--------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Two-stage least squares (Instrumental Variables).

Why IV is appropriate  
• The central threat is reverse causality—better-governed firms attract institutional investors. IV breaks this simultaneity.  
• The FactSet/LionShares data are quarterly and provide both fund-level and firm-level positions. This lets us build a powerful “shift–share” (Bartik-style) instrument that has been used extensively in the finance literature.  
• DID or event-study designs would require clearly dated, country-specific governance shocks that affect only some firms. Those shocks exist (e.g., national governance code adoptions) but they confound a clean link between ownership and governance because the reform itself may directly affect governance.  
• An RDD is not feasible because we do not observe a natural forcing variable that deterministically assigns institutional ownership.  

Instrument construction (core idea)  
Step 1: Start from Q-1 portfolio weights of each global institutional investor j in each firm i (ωij,t-1).  
Step 2: Obtain the net dollar flow into each investor/fund in quarter t (Flowj,t).  
Step 3: Predicted shares purchased in firm i in quarter t: Σj ωij,t-1 × Flowj,t.  
Step 4: Divide by firm market cap to obtain Predicted_Inst_Ownit.  

Intuition: All else equal, if CalPERS or BlackRock experiences a large inflow in 2003:Q2, any firm in which they already held 0.5 % the previous quarter will mechanically receive 0.5 % × inflow of new buying, irrespective of that firm’s contemporaneous governance. Flows are driven largely by retail capital movements, past performance, or pension contribution cycles—arguably unrelated to a particular foreign firm’s governance in that quarter.

2SLS specification  
First stage:           Inst_Ownit = α1 + β1 Predicted_Inst_Ownit + γXit + δi + φt + εit  
Second stage:   Governanceit = α2 + β2 𝐼̂nst_Ownit + γXit + δi + φt + uit  

with firm fixed effects δi and global (or country-quarter) time fixed effects φt.

--------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Treated = higher institutional ownership (% of shares held by institutions).  
This is continuous, not binary; magnitudes matter.

Control group / Counterfactual  
• The counterfactual consists of the same firm in quarters in which it would not have experienced a mechanically induced rise in institutional ownership (because flows into its pre-existing owners happened to be low or negative).  
• Firm fixed effects force identification to come from within-firm changes and thus each firm serves as its own control.

Timing  
• Quarterly change in Predicted_Inst_Own (2000:Q1-2005:Q4).  
No single event date; rather a panel of repeated exogenous shocks (fund flows).

--------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument Relevance  
Predicted_Inst_Own must be strongly correlated with actual Inst_Own. Plausible because large, sticky funds rebalance mechanically when flows arrive. Will test using first-stage F-stat (>10 rule of thumb).

A2. Exclusion Restriction  
Fund flows affect a firm’s governance only through the change in that firm’s institutional ownership, not directly. Plausible: flows are typically driven by investor contribution cycles, past fund performance, or broad macro factors, none of which directly modify firm-level governance in distant countries.

A3. No General-Equilibrium Spillovers (SUTVA)  
One firm’s mechanically induced ownership shock does not directly change another firm’s governance (beyond aggregate effects captured by quarter fixed effects). Plausible given wide dispersion across industries and the short horizon.

A4. Monotonicity  
A positive inflow into a fund cannot decrease its holdings in a firm conditional on a positive starting weight. This holds mechanically under proportional rebalancing.

A5. Data Quality & Timing  
Holdings are reported on a quarterly basis with accurate end-of-quarter dates, aligning with flows. Errors are assumed to be classical.

--------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------
T1. Strategic trading by institutions (violation of exclusion).  
Mitigation: use only “indexer” funds (identified via Lipper/CRSP) whose mandate is passive. Repeat using only largest pension funds with rigid allocation policies. Placebo: lagged flows (t-2) should not affect contemporaneous governance when inserted in the first stage.

T2. Country-level governance shocks correlated with cross-border flows.  
Mitigation: include country-quarter fixed effects which absorb any contemporaneous shock common to all firms in the same country and quarter.

T3. Weak instruments or measurement error in flows.  
Mitigation: report first-stage F-stats; winsorize extreme flow observations; instrument may be constructed alternatively at the fund-family level and at the aggregate institutional investor type (e.g., all US mutual funds) to verify robustness.

--------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # Fast data handling
library(fixest)       # High-dimensional FE & IV
library(haven)        # If Stata/other formats are needed

# 1. Data Loading -----------------------------------------------------------
# Assume three CSVs: firm-level holdings, fund-level flows, governance scores
firm_hold <- fread("firm_holdings.csv")      # firm_id, fund_id, qdate, shares
fund_flows <- fread("fund_flows.csv")        # fund_id, qdate, net_flow_usd
govern     <- fread("governance_scores.csv") # firm_id, qdate, gov_score, controls

# 2. Variable Construction --------------------------------------------------
# 2A. Predicted ownership (shift–share instrument)
# Merge t-1 holdings with current fund flows
firm_hold[, qdate_lag := shift(qdate, 1, type = "lag"), by = .(fund_id)]
setkey(firm_hold, fund_id, qdate_lag); setkey(fund_flows, fund_id, qdate)

pred <- firm_hold[fund_flows, nomatch = 0,
                  on = .(fund_id, qdate_lag = qdate),
                  allow.cartesian = TRUE]     # join

pred[, pred_shares := shares * net_flow_usd / sum(net_flow_usd), by = .(fund_id, qdate)]  # proportional

# Aggregate to firm level
firm_pred <- pred[, .(pred_inst_own = sum(pred_shares, na.rm = TRUE)),
                  by = .(firm_id, qdate)]

# 2B. Actual institutional ownership
act_inst <- firm_hold[, .(inst_shares = sum(shares)), by = .(firm_id, qdate)]

# 2C. Combine with governance and controls
dt <- merge(govern, act_inst, by = c("firm_id", "qdate"), all.x = TRUE)
dt <- merge(dt, firm_pred, by = c("firm_id", "qdate"), all.x = TRUE)

# Ownership in percent of shares outstanding
dt[, inst_own := 100 * inst_shares / shares_outstanding]
dt[, pred_inst_own := 100 * pred_inst_own / shares_outstanding]

# Winsorize 1st/99th percentiles
wins <- function(x, p=0.01){ q <- quantile(x, probs=c(p,1-p), na.rm=TRUE);
                             pmin(pmax(x,q[1]),q[2])}
dt[, `:=`(inst_own = wins(inst_own), pred_inst_own = wins(pred_inst_own))]

# 3. Main IV Regression -----------------------------------------------------
# Firm FE + Country*Quarter FE
dt[, cq_fe := paste0(country, "_", qdate)]

iv_mod <- feols(gov_score ~ 1 | firm_id + cq_fe | 
                  inst_own ~ pred_inst_own,
                data = dt, cluster = ~ firm_id)

summary(iv_mod)

# 4. Robustness Check: Passive funds only -----------------------------------
# Suppose we have a variable passive_flag in fund_flows
fund_flows_passive <- fund_flows[passive_flag == 1]
# Re-run instrument construction (steps similar to above) then:
# ... (code omitted for brevity)
# iv_mod_passive <- feols(...)
# summary(iv_mod_passive)
```

--------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------
Direction: Positive. Theory suggests institutional investors, especially cross-border and large fiduciaries, press for stronger governance to protect minority shareholders.  

Magnitude (rough prior): A one-standard-deviation (≈10 pp) exogenous rise in institutional ownership could raise a governance score by ~0.15-0.25 sd (e.g., increase board independence by 5 pp or reduce entrenchment index by 0.3 points). These are broadly in line with prior U.S.-only studies (e.g., Aggarwal et al. 2011).

--------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV Design)
--------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F>10) ………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion (no direct path from flows to governance) …… 0.5  
C3: Monotonicity (flows cannot reduce holdings) …………… 1  
C4: SUTVA / no spillovers beyond FE controls ……………… 0.5  
C5: Data accuracy & correct temporal ordering ……………… 1  
Total (out of 5) ……………………………………………………… 4.0  

The biggest residual concerns lie in the exclusion assumption (institutions may lobby regulators) and potential cross-firm spillovers. These are partly mitigated but warrant extensive robustness and placebo tests.

--------------------------------------------------
This plan leverages exogenous variation in fund inflows to isolate the causal impact of institutional ownership on governance across a global sample.
